items.title: The Devil’s Hidden Strategy: Allen Parr Reveals How Christians Become Trapped
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Author and YouTuber Allen Parr is on a mission to help people think through the spiritual barriers that could be holding them back from a fruitful life.

Parr’s new book, “Breaking Through: How Ordinary Believers Experience Extraordinary Freedom,” is all about finding freedom. He relies on his own experiences to help readers explore this essential topic.

“When I look at my life, there’s a lot of challenges … I refer to them as soul chains, but really, that’s probably a synonym for strongholds, things that hold Christians back from walking in their full potential,” he said. “As Christians, we know we’re saved, we know that we are forgiven, we know we’re on our way to Heaven, and that’s great.”

Parr said the book’s premise is Jesus died to forgive human beings for their sins, but also to offer freedom so people can live a “life of abundance.”

“I wanted to write a book to help Christians understand how they can experience the freedom and the victorious life that Jesus promised us,” he said.

Parr also spoke about why some churches might not openly speak about matters pertaining to mental health or even spiritual warfare.

“Maybe one of the reasons why a lot of churches don’t want to deal with it is that they don’t really know how to go about addressing a lot of these things,” he said. “Because, as church leaders, we’re trained in the areas of apologetics. We’re trained in the area of theology and hermeneutics and all of that. But a lot of times, we’re not trained to understand how to deal with someone who’s dealing with serious mental health issues. So oftentimes, churches may not be equipped … to know how to handle it.”

He also spoke to another dynamic: the human penchant for picking extreme “either, or” positions on demons and the supernatural.

“We err on two extremes,” Parr said. “One extreme is, ‘Hey, you know, every single thing is a demon. Everything is a demon. Everything needs to be cast out. If you’re having a bad day, that’s the demon of depression that’s attacking you,'” he said. “No, it’s just life. We have difficult days.”

The author said the notion “everything is a demon” can heighten spiritual warfare and lead some people to exaggerate or sensationalize what they or others face. That said, he pointed to the other side of the paradigm.

“The other side is the other extreme, and that’s the fact that, ‘Hey, we’re not in a spiritual war. There is no such thing as demons and supernatural … and you just need to work everything out by yourself.”

Parr encouraged Christians to find common ground in the middle of these extremes, and pointed to the words of Ephesians 6 to make his point — a chapter in the Bible that discusses the wrestling humans face against spiritual powers.

He spoke about his own struggles and the “soul chains” so many people struggle with, including lust, among other issues. He believes these soul chains are sometimes formed as a result of emotional wounds.

“I struggled with toxic relationships, having grown up in a home where there was a lot of divorce,” Parr said. “My mom and dad got divorced multiple times over, and that created a fear in me to get into a committed relationship and a committed marriage.”

He said the devil often seizes upon these soul wounds to open up emotional pain. Parr said divorce created a chain of fear over getting married. He also had father wounds as his dad was around in his life but not living in his home.

“I talk about the soul chain of perfectionism, and I struggled with that,” he continued. “Lots of different things, a poverty mentality because we grew up without much money, and so all of these things are things that we don’t even realize a lot of times until we’re in our later stages of life.”

A lot of these issues are built on deception and will hold people back, he said.

“Every soul chain is established on some sort of lie that the enemy would want you to believe instead of the truth,” Parr said.

He believes it’s essential to pinpoint the “chains” holding people back so that they can be dealt with. Part of that process is having people in life who individuals are close with; these people can then raise issues they observe.

“So the question is, whenever people bring certain things up to you, like, ‘Hey, you’re dealing with perfectionism,’ or ‘Hey, I see this issue of anger in your life, or unforgiveness, or shame, low self-esteem,’ I mean, there’s a ton of them that I talk about in the book,” Parr said. “The question is, do you receive that, or are you resistant to that? Oftentimes, if we’re resistant, that’s a sign that maybe this thing has a chain and a hold on us that we’re not realizing.”

After identifying these ties, he said, “Breaking Through: How Ordinary Believers Experience Extraordinary Freedom,” offers an opportunity to explore a biblical roadmap to help walk toward freedom.

items.title: ‘They’re Demonic’: Astronaut Who Walked on the Moon on Shocking Truth About Aliens
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "That's ... what God showed me."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Former astronaut Charlie Duke is known for being the youngest man to walk on the moon. But Duke, 91, is also a strong Christian who has a fascinating perspective on aliens and UFOs, subjects that have received a plethora of attention of late.

The astronaut, who was the spacecraft communicator for the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969 and spent 265 hours in space during that time, told CBN News he once wasn’t so sure about his beliefs on the true nature of aliens and UFOs.

“For a long time [years ago] I was praying about UFOs, and asked for a sign,” Duke said. “I felt like UFOs were demonic … but I was saying that at rotary clubs and stuff like that, and people were laughing me off the stage.”

So, he asked the Lord to help him come to a definitive conclusion that would settle the matter once and for all.

“I said, ‘God, if I’m really right about this, then give me a sign tomorrow morning that a very good friend of mine at breakfast will start talking about UFOs,'” he said. “And this guy’s a businessman. He never talks about science stuff or … stuff like that. So the next morning at breakfast, we sat down, he said, ‘Charlie, come on over. I wanna start talking to you about UFOs.'”

Duke interpreted this as an answer to his prayer. The former astronaut then appealed to Scripture to make his case, looking at the Bible’s description of Satan to further conclude his position.

“The Lord says what we’re seeing is real, but the devil can appear as an angel of light, the Bible says,” he said. “And so what I believe … is the UFOs are trying to turn us away from the truth and run after these alien beings, which are really not beings at all. They’re demonic.”

Ultimately, Duke said he’s unconcerned with those who might laugh at him or mock his perspective on the matter.

“You can laugh at me if you want to, but that’s … what God showed me, and I’m sticking to it,” he said.

Duke said he never personally viewed anything on his flight to the moon that would be considered alien or UFO-like. Watch the interview above for more.

items.title: After the Washington Wizards Lost to the Raptors, They Invited Scottie Barnes Into Their Prayer Circle
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: In the NBA, the postgame TV interview moves fast. The horn sounds, the star of the night gets steered toward the sideline and a reporter is waiting with a microphone before he’s caught his breath. After the Toronto Raptors beat the Washington Wizards 112-102 on Friday, Oct. 23, the microphone was re
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

In the NBA, the postgame TV interview moves fast. The horn sounds, the star of the night gets steered toward the sideline and a reporter is waiting with a microphone before he’s caught his breath.

After the Toronto Raptors beat the Washington Wizards 112-102 on Friday, Oct. 23, the microphone was ready. But Scottie Barnes was walking across midcourt with a Gatorade towel over his head, headed for the Wizards’ postgame prayer circle.

A player in the Washington group waved him over. Barnes stepped in among forward Anthony Gill and a handful of Wizards players, and the circle closed around him.

Barnes, Toronto’s 25-year-old forward and a former NBA Rookie of the Year, had just finished with 28 points, 14 rebounds and five assists.

Toronto’s TV broadcast, meanwhile, was holding for him.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Bleacher Report (@bleacherreport)

“He just took off,” one of the Raptors’ broadcasters said as Barnes joined the huddle. “So we’ll wait a minute for him to return.”

A few seconds later, the call caught up to the picture: Barnes was “in the huddle there with the Wizards players, sharing a prayer as the Toronto Raptors come away with this victory.”

When the circle broke, there were hugs all around, and Barnes started back across the floor with the towel around his neck. “Here comes Scottie,” the broadcast said, sending it down to the sideline. The microphone was still waiting.

Gill, in his seventh season with Washington, was one of five finalists for the J. Walter Kennedy Citizenship Award in 2024, which NBA writers give for community service.

He has talked publicly about his faith, too. Sharing the stage with Orlando Magic forward Jonathan Isaac at Liberty University’s convocation in 2024, he told students that people assume an NBA player has “it all figured out.”

“They assume that just because you’ve been blessed with a lot of money, life should be easy,” he said. He also said, “I tell myself I need to be more like Jesus. And what was Jesus? The ultimate servant. So, I serve the people around me.”

items.title: The Glory of God’s Worship
items.author: Thomas J. Kronholz
items.summary:
Thomas J. Kronholz

The self-affirmations of secularism will not suffice for us to recognize the mystery of our making in God.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Thomas J. Kronholz

Its walls breached and temple razed, Jerusalem, the city of God’s worship, was laid to waste by the destructive power of Babylon. In the aftermath of this disaster, Baruch prophesied its meaning, reproving Israel for her infidelity while promising her redemption. These twin themes color his message as he contrasts the ruinous effects of idolatry with the glory of godly worship. Escalating toward an apocalyptic vision of their exaltation, Baruch reveals a new and hallowed name for God’s people, indicating their identity: “your name shall be named forever by God: the peace of justice, the glory of God’s worship [δόξα θεοσεβείας]” (Bar 5:4 NABRE).

Modern life, marked as it is by competing philosophies and challenges to the faith, shares similar social confusions as pre-exilic Israel. Uprooted from a culture of established worship, modern man has become uncertain of his creation and calling. Seeking meaning, he exchanges earthly causes and material pursuits, each betraying him. Our call nevertheless remains the same as those Israelites who were urged to renounce idolatry and to recover their vocation in right worship. In this sense must each Christian lay claim to his authentic identity and exalted name bestowed by God, “Righteous Peace, Godly Glory,” (Bar 5:4) which he shares in and through Christ, the true temple.

The modern project of secularism, which exiled God from the public sphere, has produced new forms of idolatry, fracturing society—a reality reflected in man’s own interior life. In this sense is our cultural crisis of identity mirrored in man himself. No longer grounded in his faithful foundation, man pours himself into countless forms, constructing his identity from below, rather than receiving it from above. Because these mutable identities are unstable, the contemporary mind is often plagued by anxiety and despair. 

Whereas idolatry scatters man’s powers and personality—so vividly shown in Israel’s own exile—right worship produces unity. Notably, this unity is not only an outward communion among peoples, but an interior integration within one’s own self. Gathered from such dispersion, man recovers himself, worshipping in spirit and truth. This implies integration within Christ’s own body of sacrifice and therefore also entails one’s own self-gift.

It is well known that Christ is high priest and perfect sacrifice, the one who offers and is offered at each Holy Mass, though our participation in this twofold role of priest and victim is often less considered. Baptized into the universal priesthood, each of us is privileged to partake in that Eucharistic liturgy wherein the priest, acting in the person of Christ the head, offers “my sacrifice and yours” to God the Father, as we the laity, the very members of Christ’s body, unite ourselves to this sacrificial action. In this way do Christians fulfill St. Peter’s command to be “built into a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Pet 2:5). Though the ordained priest acts in an order altogether distinct from the laity, the baptized all rightly participate in the Eucharistic offering, donating their very lives and selves together with Christ’s sacrifice.

As Christ is offered to God the Father at the Mass, his members are likewise called to be conformed to and included in this sacrifice. For this reason, St. Paul commands Christians to “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Rom 12:1). Worshipping in “spirit and truth” (John 4:24), Christians are gathered in Christ’s spirit and incorporated in the temple of his body. Thus united to his sacrifice, we are jointly offered at the Mass, realizing spiritual worship. 

By this wholly unique act, man may discover his authentic identity, for this mystery is not manifest by consumption, conformism, nor capitulation to passions—that is, self-enclosed acts of idolatry—but by realizing his rational capacity for love, which in a composite being of body and soul implies some manner of embodied self-giving. This way of heroic love was forged by Christ upon the cross, a deed made sacrament in the Eucharistic gift.

That man’s identity may be evinced in worship is a mystery that may be contemplated in light of the ground of reality itself—that is to say, the Trinity. For we may observe that the identity of God the Son, who existed from all eternity, is realized in relation to God the Father. Indeed, each of the persons of the Trinity is constituted as relations: Each is a self-communication, as it were, to the other. 

The Son alone, however, took on flesh, drawing his humanity into the self-giving dynamic proper to his person. This profound reality is manifest in the sacrificial action of the cross, wherein his humanity bears witness to his donative love. Responding to this gratuitous love, our call is to graft ourselves into Christ’s Body of worship, finding ourselves in this self-giving act. Caught up in Christ’s self-offering, our false selves fall away, even as our own weak love is purified and our own dim vision clarified. United to him in Holy Communion, we become one body, confirming our identity.

Order Your Set Today

As they simply are relations, the Trinitarian Persons would not be themselves, so to speak, apart from their self-giving communication. Accordingly, man is not made to be a self-enclosed monad but one in self-giving relationship. The act of worship allows man to break forth from the prison of self; it actualizes his radical potency for self-communication, which must be fulfilled for him to be himself. 

Idolatry turns man inward as he focuses on consumption and control: the consumption of sense goods and the control of all things. True worship, however, reverses this paradigm, drawing man from himself so that he yields to God, seeking him for his own sake. The path to the divine is thus one of renunciation and surrender. In right worship—that integrated act of self-gift which takes place in and through the Son—we respond to that love with which the Father first loved us, offering him thanksgiving in Christ. In this act, we are conformed to the Son, realizing our identities in his body of self-giving love. Reflecting on these themes, St. Augustine connects the mystery of the Christian identity to the mystery of faith, writing:

If you are the body of Christ and its very members, then the Mystery of your identity is upon the Lord’s table. You receive the Mystery of the Lord, responding “amen” to what you are, and by responding, assent. As you hear, “the body of Christ,” you respond, “amen.” Be then a member of Christ’s body that your “amen” may be true.

Modern culture often thinks itself beyond idolatry, viewing the infidelity of societies such as pre-exilic Israel as historical ignorance. Nevertheless, modern observance of the Lord’s Day has been forsaken by the greater part of humanity as man invests himself in creation. In this way does contemporary man practice far graver idolatry, rejecting the revelation of the Incarnate God, choosing exile. Notably, all such idolatry effaces one’s identity; the undue honor of created things degrades man, reducing him to their level. For this reason, the Psalmist sings: 

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but they do not speak; they have eyes, but they do not see; they have ears, but they do not hear, and there is no breath in their mouths. Those who make them and all who trust them shall become like them (Ps 135:15-18).

By contrast, St. Paul says of Christians: “Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch, as you really are unleavened. For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7). Remarkably, Christians are said to be unleavened because of Christ’s sacrifice. As sin is a foreign agent, incompatible with both nature and grace, it must be cast out that man may recover his true face. This reality takes place by uniting oneself to Christ’s sacrifice, present daily upon the altars of the Church.

Observing the dictates associated with the Lord’s Day, man is gathered from the dispersion of his powers and from the world so that his heart may rest recollected in adoration. Living an integrated life of sacrificial worship, Christians may fulfill their call to become the “praise of his glory” (Eph 1:12) and the “glory of God’s worship” (Bar 5:4 NABRE), rejecting the dark allures of idolatry. Eucharistic Prayer IV in the Roman Missal summarizes these themes in a single sentence:

Look, O Lord, upon the Sacrifice which you yourself have provided for your Church, and grant . . . to all who partake of this one Bread and one Chalice that, gathered into one body by the Holy Spirit, they may truly become a living sacrifice in Christ to the praise of your glory.” (emphasis added)

The self-affirmations of secularism will not suffice for us to recognize the mystery of our making in God. Nor will self-referential worship draw us from ourselves, revealing our relational nature. Until we lay our hearts prostrate in perfect praise and self-offering, they will never be manifest, remaining self-contained and hidden. It is not in self-satisfaction but in self-offering that we discover that profound mystery of our identity in Christ as he foretold, “Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matt 16:25). 

In worship, our ineffable identity is revealed as a mysterious member of Christ. Made by him and for him, made anew in him and into him, we find ourselves by giving ourselves to God. In this way is our prophetic call and identity realized as the “glory of God’s worship.”

items.title: Monday, October 26, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus heals a woman who had been crippled for eighteen years.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ephesians 4:32–5:8

And be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you. Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and live in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.

But fornication and impurity of any kind, or greed, must not even be mentioned among you, as is proper among saints. Entirely out of place is obscene, silly, and vulgar talk; but instead, let there be thanksgiving. Be sure of this, that no fornicator or impure person, or one who is greedy (that is, an idolater), has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes on those who are disobedient. Therefore do not be associated with them. For once you were darkness, but now in the Lord you are light. Live as children of light.

Psalm
Psalm 1:1-2, 3, 4, 6

Happy are those
    who do not follow the advice of the wicked,
or take the path that sinners tread,
    or sit in the seat of scoffers;
but their delight is in the law of the Lord,
    and on his law they meditate day and night.
They are like trees
    planted by streams of water,
which yield their fruit in its season,
    and their leaves do not wither.
In all that they do, they prosper.
The wicked are not so,
    but are like chaff that the wind drives away.
for the Lord watches over the way of the righteous,
    but the way of the wicked will perish.

Gospel Reading
Luke 13:10-17

Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the sabbath. And just then there appeared a woman with a spirit that had crippled her for eighteen years. She was bent over and was quite unable to stand up straight. When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said, “Woman, you are set free from your ailment.” When he laid his hands on her, immediately she stood up straight and began praising God. But the leader of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had cured on the sabbath, kept saying to the crowd, “There are six days on which work ought to be done; come on those days and be cured, and not on the sabbath day.” But the Lord answered him and said, “You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger, and lead it away to give it water? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen long years, be set free from this bondage on the sabbath day?” When he said this, all his opponents were put to shame; and the entire crowd was rejoicing at all the wonderful things that he was doing.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus heals a woman who had been crippled for eighteen years. Can we see the power that flows from faith in rather obvious and spectacular ways?

Going back to Jesus himself, of course, and up through so many of the saints in the tradition, you will see the power of faith manifested in healing. It’s as though a Christian becomes a conduit of the divine power, as though God’s power, which creates and sustains the cosmos, can flow through the person of faith for healing.

We can also experience spiritual healing of the soul. Its source is the energy, the power, the Spirit, the new being, that appeared in and through Jesus Christ. We heal the soul by bringing to bear the salvator, the healer, the one who in his person reconciled God and us, who opened the soul to the divine power. Where is this new being available? In Scripture, the liturgy, and the sacraments.
